title: The History of Oranges — The Fruit That Named a Colour
fullText: For a thousand years, the English language had no word for the color orange. Sunsets, autumn leaves, the glow of a campfire, all of it was just called yellow, red. Then a piece of fruit arrived from the other side of the world and gave an entire color its name. No other [music] fruit has ever done that. Not the lemon, not the cherry, not the plum. Only the orange rewrote the dictionary. So, how did a small bitter citrus that started in [music] the jungles of ancient Asia end up on the breakfast tables of 300 million Americans inside the medicine chests of the Royal Navy and in the heated palaces of French kings who spent fortunes just to keep the trees alive through winter? That story starts roughly 8 million years ago in the foothills where the Himalayas meet the jungles of Southeast Asia. This is the region where modern-day [music] Asam in northeast India, northern Myanmar, and the Yunan [music] province of western China all converge. According to genetic research conducted by citrus biologists, this narrow corridor of land is where every citrus [music] species on the planet originated. Lemons, limes, grapefruits, tangerines, pomelos, and yes, oranges. They all trace their ancestry back to this one strip of territory wedged between mountains and monsoons. Wild citrus grew in these forests for millions of years before any human being took notice [music] of it. And when they finally did, the fruit was not exactly appetizing. [music] The wild ancestors of the modern orange were small, seedy, and often unbearably sour [music] or bitter. They looked nothing like the plump, sweet fruit you would recognize today, but they carried something inside [music] them that would eventually change the course of human navigation, warfare, and medicine. Vitamin C. Nobody would understand that connection for thousands of years. [music] But the molecule was there, locked inside the rind, quietly waiting. The first citrus species to travel westward was the citroron, a lumpy, thick-skinned fruit that made its way to Persia and the eastern Mediterranean around the fourth and fifth centuries BC. The Greeks and Romans valued [music] it mostly for medicine and perfume, not as food. Lemons followed not long after, reaching Rome by the late 1st century BC. But the orange itself, the fruit that would eventually eclipse every other citrus, took a very different path. The sweet orange that we eat today [music] did not exist in the wild. It was a hybrid, a cross between a mandarin and a pomelo. And that crossing [music] happened somewhere in southern China or northern Indochina thousands of years ago. Chinese farmers cultivated it, refined it over generations, [music] and turned it into something worth trading. And along the ancient roots connecting East Asia to the Middle East, the orange began a journey that would take centuries and span entire continents. The word itself is a fossil of that [music] journey. The original name for the orange tree comes from Sanskrit, the classical language of the Indian subcontinent. The word was naranga and it likely traces even further back to a Dravidian root, possibly Tamil, [music] Nurga, meaning fragrant. As the fruit moved west along trade routes, the word traveled with it, shapeshifting in every new language it touched. Persian traders adopted it as narang. Arabic merchants carried it further and called it narang. When it reached medieval Italy, regional dialects rendered it as naransia or naranza. The old French became orange as in the phrase pom [music] dorenge literally meaning orange apple and somewhere along the way [music] the leading n got dropped. Linguists believe that happened because speakers confused the N of the fruit with [music] the N in the French article un. So unarange became unarange and then unor eventually [music] in English just orange. A word that had started in the forests of India arrived in England with the fingerprints [music] of six different languages still on it. But the fruit that carried this name through the Moorish conquest of Spain was not the sweet variety most people picture today. In 711 AD, Islamic [music] Arab and Berber forces crossed the straight of Gibralta from North Africa into the Iberian Peninsula. Over the following years, they conquered most of what is now Spain and Portugal. And they brought with them advances in mathematics, astronomy, irrigation [music] engineering, paper, and among their agricultural imports, the bitter orange. Arab and Persian gardeners had been [music] growing bitter orange trees across the Middle East and North Africa for generations. They praised the trees for their fragrance, their ornamental [music] beauty, and their use in traditional medicine. The fruit itself was too sharp and too sour [music] to eat raw, but the blossoms smelled extraordinary, and the peel could be turned into perfumes, preserves, and medicinal preparations. By the 9th century, the Moors had introduced the bitter [music] orange to Sicily during the Muslim conquest of the island. Complex irrigation systems designed specifically for citrus orchards began appearing across the [music] Mediterranean. For roughly 500 years, this bitter ornamental citrus was the only orange that [music] Europe knew. And honestly, Europeans were not that impressed. They treated it as a curiosity, [music] a medicine, a garden decoration, not as a fruit worth eating. That was about to change. In the late 1400s and early 1500s, Portuguese sailors were pushing further down the coast of Africa and across the Indian Ocean than any European had gone before. These voyages were brutal. When Vasco Dama set sail from Lisbon in 1497 with four ships and 170 men, he was sailing into the unknown. The voyage around the Cape of Good Hope was one of the most dangerous maritime passages on Earth. Storms battered the fleet, supplies ran low, and Scurvy, though nobody understood what caused it yet, was already beginning to kill his crew. By the time the expedition reached the trading ports along the East African coast, Dama had already lost dozens of men. But along those Arab trade routes that [music] connected India to the African coast, his crew encountered something remarkable. A sweeter, juicier variety of orange that Arab merchants had been moving between India, China, and the ports of East Africa for years. Nobody on [music] the Portuguese ships had ever tasted anything like it. Dagama brought samples back [music] to Portugal, and they were a sensation. This was not the sharp medicinal fruit the moors had planted across Spain centuries earlier. This was something you actually wanted to bite into. The sweet orange thrived in the warm climate of southern Portugal, particularly in the Algav region where sunny days and mild winters created ideal growing conditions. It spread across the country so quickly and so successfully that within a century it had [music] become known throughout Europe simply as the Portugal orange. And that name cemented itself in ways most English speakers never realize. In Greek, the word for orange is still Portoali. In Turkish, Portal. In Romanian, Portoalu. In Arabic, Bertal. Half the languages [music] on the Mediterranean rim named this fruit after the country that delivered it to their shores. Meanwhile, the Germans took a completely different approach. They called the sweet orange apple scene and the Dutch called it sinn apple. Both names translate to the same thing, Chinese apple. Because even though the Portuguese brought the fruit to Europe, everybody knew where it really came from. Now, here is where the story does something that no other fruit in history has managed. [music] It renamed a color. Before sweet oranges became widely available in Europe in the 1500s, the English language had no standalone word for the color between red and yellow. For nearly a thousand years, English speakers had relied on the old English compound word geol red, which translates [music] literally to yellow red. That was the best anyone could do. It described the hue by its relationship to two other colors, not as a color [music] in its own right. When Jeffrey Chaucser sat down to write the Canterbury Tales in the 1390s, he needed to describe the color of a fox in his story, The Nun's Priest's Tale. The best he could manage was [music] to call the animals fur the color between yellow and red. He had no single word for it. Nobody writing in English at that [music] time did. Colors that we would now call orange were described as saffron, citrine, amber, tory, [music] or red gold, depending on the shade and the context. None of those words meant what orange means today. They were workarounds, borrowed terms from spices, gemstones, and fabrics. The color existed everywhere in nature in sunsets and autumn leaves [music] and the coats of animals. But the English language simply had no dedicated name for it. Then the fruit showed up in English markets and slowly, almost accidentally, the word for the fruit crossed over into the word for the color. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the first recorded use of orange as a color name in English appeared in 1512. Someone used it in a will, spelling it orange. By 1532, the phrase orange velvet was appearing in Scottish account books. Through the late 1500s, orange tory showed up regularly in clothing [music] records and textile inventories. The transition happened gradually over about a century until by the 1600s the word orange as a color name was widespread. [music] And then came the moment that made it permanent when Isaac Newton conducted his famous prism experiments in the late 1660s and 1670s [music] and mapped the visible spectrum of light. He identified seven distinct colors in [music] the rainbow. red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. [music] Orange had earned its official place in the scientific vocabulary [music] of color. Think about that for a second. A fruit had filled a gap in human language that had been [music] empty for a millennium. We see that color every single day in sunsets, in flames, [music] in the fur of foxes, in the embers of a dying fire. And for a thousand years, we [music] just called it yellow red because we had no better word. The orange gave [music] us one. But this fruit was not just reshaping how people talked. It was reshaping how the wealthy and powerful displayed their status. By the 16th and 17th centuries, the sweet orange had become one of the most coveted luxury items in all of Europe. In London during [music] the 1500s, a single orange could cost as much as a pair of shoes. The fruit was rare, imported, perishable, and completely impossible to grow outdoors [music] in the cold, wet climates of Northern Europe, which is exactly what made it the perfect status symbol. If you could afford oranges, you could afford anything. And if you could [music] grow your own orange trees in a climate where they had no business surviving, you were making a statement about your wealth and your [music] control over nature itself. Across the continent from Florence to Fontenblau, wealthy aristocrats began building elaborate heated [music] structures called oreries designed specifically to shelter citrus trees through the winter months. It was considered good manners [music] to present your king with an orange tree as a gift, a gesture of flattery that acknowledged citrus as the healthy luxury of the age. These oreries were not simple green houses. They were architectural monuments to excess and nobody built a more extravagant ory than Louis I 14th of France. In 1663 the palace of Versailles received its first oryer designed by the architect Louie [music] Lavo. But 20 years later the king decided it was not grand enough. He commissioned Jules Hardwin Mansard to build something far more ambitious. The new oryer completed between 1684 and 1686 was massive. The central gallery stretched over 150 m long with barrel vaulted ceilings rising 13 m high. The walls were nearly 5 m thick, designed to trap heat and maintain a temperature above 5° [music] C, even in the dead of a French winter. Louisie filled it with orange trees gathered [music] from every royal residence in France, plus hundreds more imported from Italy, Spain, and [music] Portugal. And then came the Fukquet affair. In 1664, when Louieie [music] disgraced his former finance minister, Nicholas Fukquet, and convicted [music] him of corruption, the king seized over 1,000 orange trees from Fukquet's private estate [music] at Vol Vikt and had every last one of them carted to Versailles. By the 1790s, the Versailles Orangeerie held several thousand trees, some of them over 200 years old, [music] and it was the largest collection of its kind anywhere in Europe. But it was never really [music] about the fruit. Oranges at Versailles served as three-dimensional propaganda. Foreign diplomats and [music] rival monarchs visiting the palace would witness Louis the 14th's ability [music] to defy winter itself. If this king could force Mediterranean trees to bloom [music] in the frost of northern France, what else was he capable of? Courtiers brought orange trees as gifts to win royal favor. The king reportedly [music] had his favorites potted in solid silver tubs and placed throughout the stateooms of the palace to perfume the air because he [music] had developed an allergy to flowers in old age and preferred the scent of citrus instead. A fruit that started as a wild bitter thing in the jungles of Asia had become the ultimate ornament of European royal excess. While kings were spending fortunes keeping orange trees alive for decoration, the fruit was about to prove its value in a way that had nothing to do with luxury. It was about to save thousands of lives. For centuries, [music] sailors on long ocean voyages had been dying from a mysterious and devastating disease called scurvy. The symptoms were horrifying. Skin bruised at the slightest touch. Gums bled and swelled until teeth loosened and fell out. Hair fell away. Old wounds that had healed years earlier would suddenly reopen. Left untreated, victims declined into lethargy and death. And the scale of the killing was staggering. The British Navy alone lost an estimated 1 million sailors to scurvy between [music] 1500 and 1800. That death toll exceeded all British combat fatalities over the same three centuries. Vasco Dama's first voyage to India lost roughly 100 of his 170 crew members, most of them to scurvy. Mellin's circumnavigation of the globe lost [music] over 80% of its men, with scurvy responsible for the majority. Sailors had been noticing for centuries that eating citrus seemed to help. The English Admiral Richard Hawkins specifically recommended [music] oranges and lemons for scurvy as early as 1593. The English naval surgeon John Woodall made the same recommendation in his 1617 manual, The Surgeon's Mate. But the knowledge never stuck. [music] It kept getting discovered, then forgotten, then discovered again. Nobody formalized the connection. Then in 1747, a Scottish naval surgeon named James Lind changed that. Aboard the HMS Salsbury in the English Channel. Lind conducted what many historians now consider the first controlled clinical trial in the [music] history of medicine. He selected 12 sailors suffering from scurvy and divided [music] them into six pairs. Each pair received a different treatment. The first got cider, the second received dilute sulfuric acid, the third vinegar, the fourth sea water, the fifth a paste made from garlic and mustard seed. And the sixth pair received two oranges and one lemon each day. After 6 days, only the pair eating citrus showed any [music] improvement, and their recovery was dramatic. The other 10 men showed nothing. Lind published his findings in 1753. The results were clear, but the British Navy did not officially adopt citrus rations for another 42 [music] years, not until 1795. That is nearly half a century of sailors dying from a disease with a proven cure. Because the institutions [music] in charge moved too slowly when the Navy finally mandated a daily ration of lemon juice [music] for every sailor, scurvy virtually disappeared from British ships within a year. The less effective lime juice that [music] eventually replaced lemons is the reason British people are still called limeies to this day. While citrus was saving lives at sea, the orange was also putting down roots across the Atlantic. Christopher Columbus brought orange seeds with him on his second voyage in 1493 and planted the first trees on the island of Hispanola in what is now Haiti. Spanish [music] and Portuguese colonizers spread the fruit throughout Central and South America over the following decades, and the trees naturalized in the tropical [music] climate almost effortlessly. Brazil, in particular, became an orange paradise. Its warm, humid air and rich soil [music] producing fruit that rivaled anything growing in Portugal or Sicily. But the single most important event in the history of oranges in the Western Hemisphere happened quietly with no fanfare at all. On the grounds of a monastery in the Brazilian state of Bajia, sometime around 1820, an ordinary selector orange tree in the monastery orchard did something strange. One of its branches spontaneously mutated. Biologists call this a sport, a random genetic glitch that produces a branch with different characteristics from the rest of the tree. The fruit from that mutant [music] branch looked almost normal from the outside, except for one thing. At the base of each orange, opposite the stem, a small secondary fruit was growing inside the primary one, creating a dimple on the outside that looked [music] like a human belly button, a navl. The mutation also made the fruit completely seedless, sweet, juicy, easy to peel, and seedless. [music] It was in almost every way the perfect eating orange. But the seedlessness [music] came with a catch that would define the fruit's entire future. A seedless fruit cannot reproduce on its own. It cannot grow from seed because it produces no seeds. The only way to grow more naval oranges was to cut [music] a branch from the mutant tree and graft it onto the rootstock of another citrus tree. Which means every naval orange in the world today, every single one [music] you have ever peeled at your kitchen table is a genetic clone of that one freak branch in a Brazilian monastery 200 years ago. That mutation could have easily died out. One bad [music] storm, one disease, one neglectful gardener, and the naval orange would have vanished from history [music] before anyone outside Baja ever tasted one. Instead, it was propagated, carefully tended, and eventually carried across the ocean. Around 1870, about a dozen cutings from the original tree were sent to the United States Department [music] of Agriculture in Washington, D.C. C. The department propagated them and in 1873 shipped starter trees to growers in Florida and California for testing. One of the [music] people who received those trees was Eliza Tibbitz, a spiritualist and women's suffrage activist living in Riverside, California. Tibbitz planted her trees in her backyard garden and watered them, according to [music] local legend, with dishwater from her kitchen. The trees thrived in the warm, dry California [music] climate. The fruit they produced was sweet, seedless, easy to peel, [music] and it ripened during the mild winter months when other fresh produce was hard to come by. Word [music] spread fast. Tibbitz began selling budstock at $5 per bud, a steep price at the time, and other [music] growers rushed to plant their own naval groves across Southern California. [music] Within 25 years, the orange industry had transformed Riverside from a small agricultural settlement into the wealthiest city per capita in the entire United States. Orange groves blanketed the hillsides for miles. Wealthy investors from the east coast and even from Europe poured money [music] into land and infrastructure. The city's so-called orange barons built stately Victorian mansions [music] and imposing commercial buildings with their citrus profits. Riverside became a showcase of what a single crop could do to an economy when the conditions were right. The completion of the transcontinental railroad made it possible to ship California oranges to markets across the country and demand exploded. [music] By 1893, citrus farmers had organized the Southern California Fruit Exchange, a grower cooperative that would eventually rebrand itself as Sunkist, one of the most recognized names in American agriculture. All of it from two trees planted by a suffragist watered with dish water. That is one of those details that sounds made up, but it is not. But even as California became synonymous with oranges in the public imagination, the real volume was quietly building 1500 m to the east in Florida. And it was Florida, not California, that would turn orange juice from a seasonal luxury into a daily American ritual. Because for most of human history, people ate oranges. [music] They did not drink them. That distinction matters more than it sounds. Squeezing an orange for its juice was simple enough, but fresh juice spoiled within hours and could not be stored, shipped, or sold at any meaningful scale. A glass of fresh orange juice was something you made at home right before [music] you drank it, and only when oranges were in season. That limitation held for centuries and kept juice from ever becoming a mass market product. Then the 20th century broke [music] it wide open. After World War II, frozen concentrated orange juice exploded in popularity. Minute Made pioneered the product and between 1948 and 1949, their sales increased by 300%. The equivalent of hundreds of millions of cans. But the frozen concentrate had a problem. It tasted like [music] frozen concentrate. You had to mix it with water and the result never quite captured what a fresh orange tasted like. [music] In 1947, an Italian immigrant named Anthony Rossy had founded a small fruit packing business in Bradenton, Florida. He started by shipping gift boxes [music] of citrus to customers in the Northeast. But Rossi saw something bigger. He believed Americans wanted juice that tasted fresh, not reconstituted. In 1954, he developed a process called flash pasteurization, which heated the juice just long enough to preserve it without destroying the flavor. The result was Tropicana Pure Premium, the first commercially successful, not from concentrate, chilled orange juice. It was a genuine breakthrough. By the 1970s, Tropicana was running its own refrigerated freight trains from Florida to the Northeast, and the brand eventually captured nearly 40% of the chilled juice market. The idea of orange juice [music] at breakfast, which we now treat as something that has always existed, is really a product of mid-century American food processing and marketing. A century earlier, nobody drank orange juice with their eggs. The notion of a glass of OJ as part of a complete breakfast was manufactured [music] literally and culturally by companies that figured out how to put perishable citrus into a shelf stable product and then convinced [music] an entire country it belonged on the morning table next to the toast and the coffee. Today, Brazil produces roughly 30% of the world's oranges. The global citrus industry spans 114 countries and the fruit occupies over 3.6 [music] million hectares of farmland worldwide. The orange went from royal luxury to commodity in about 400 years. And maybe that is the strangest part of this entire story. A fruit that spent 8 million [music] years evolving in the Himalayan foothills that carried a Sanskrit name across six languages before English got hold of it. that renamed a color humans had been [music] seeing every day since the beginning of sight but had never been able to name. that traveled with the Moors into Spain and with Portuguese sailors around the Cape of Good Hope, that kings hoarded in silver tubs and naval surgeons prescribed to dying [music] men that mutated on a single branch in a Brazilian monastery and was cloned into billions of copies spread across every inhabited continent that built a billiondoll industry in California from two trees watered with kitchen scraps. That fruit now sits in a plastic bag at the grocery store for a few dollars and [music] nobody gives it a second thought. We peel them absent-mindedly. We squeeze them into glasses without looking. We toss the rind into the trash without any [music] awareness of the 8,000-year chain of events that put that particular fruit in our hands. The orange is not just something [music] you eat. It is a map of human civilization drawn in peel and pulp and juice, [music] connecting Sanskrit scholars and Portuguese explorers and French kings and British surgeons and Brazilian monks and California suffragists across millennia. [music] The next time you peel one, hold it for a second. Feel the oil mist from the rind. That scent traveled further than most people will in their entire lives.
